items.stem: Which of the following best describes "nutrition transition"?
options: Land used for growing crops that are replanted after each harvest
The shift in diets as incomes rise, from staples towards more meat, dairy, sugar, oils and processed foods
The total volume of freshwater used to produce the goods and services consumed by an individual, business or country
Living on less than the World Bank's international poverty line, US$2.15 per person per day at 2017 PPP (revised to US$3.00 at 2021 PPP in 2025)
items.answer: The shift in diets as incomes rise, from staples towards more meat, dairy, sugar, oils and processed foods
items.markingKey: B. "nutrition transition" is the shift in diets as incomes rise, from staples towards more meat, dairy, sugar, oils and processed foods.

items.stem: Sana writes: "Extreme poverty has been reduced equally in all world regions." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Most of the reduction occurred in East and South Asia; in sub-Saharan Africa the number of extremely poor people rose for decades.
items.markingKey: Most of the reduction occurred in East and South Asia; in sub-Saharan Africa the number of extremely poor people rose for decades. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain the difference between total consumption and consumption per capita.
items.answer: Per-capita consumption is the average used by each person; total consumption is per-capita use multiplied by population - China's total is large even though per-capita use is below the USA's.
items.markingKey: Per-capita consumption is the average used by each person; total consumption is per-capita use multiplied by population - China's total is large even though per-capita use is below the USA's. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Briefly explain why poverty reduction has been uneven between world regions.
items.answer: East Asia grew rapidly through export manufacturing and investment, while sub-Saharan Africa had slower growth, high population growth, conflict and commodity dependence; by 2019 most of the extremely poor lived in sub-Saharan Africa.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: East Asia grew rapidly through export manufacturing and investment, while sub-Saharan Africa had slower growth, high population growth, conflict and commodity dependence; by 2019 most of the extremely poor lived in sub-Saharan Africa. items.stem: Nia writes: "The middle class lives mainly in Europe and North America." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Most of the new global middle class is in Asia, especially China and India.
items.markingKey: Most of the new global middle class is in Asia, especially China and India. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: China: ecological footprint ≈ 3.6 gha/person; biocapacity ≈ 0.9 gha/person. World biocapacity is about 1.6 gha per person. Calculate (a) the ecological balance per person and (b) how many Earths would be needed if everyone lived like the average resident.
items.answer: (a) -2.7 gha per person (ecological deficit) (b) 3.6 / 1.6 ≈ 2.2 Earths
items.markingKey: (a) M1 biocapacity − footprint, A1 -2.7 gha and correct label. (b) M1 A1 2.2 Earths.

items.stem: Using data, describe changes in resource consumption that accompany rising incomes in a named country.
items.answer: e.g. China: meat consumption rose from about 20 kg per person in 1990 to about 60 kg; car ownership rose from very few to about 300 million vehicles; electricity use per capita increased more than fivefold.
items.markingKey: e.g. China: meat consumption rose from about 20 kg per person in 1990 to about 60 kg; car ownership rose from very few to about 300 million vehicles; electricity use per capita increased more than fivefold.

items.answer: The footprint measures demand on nature (gha needed for consumption and wastes); biocapacity measures nature's supply (gha of productive land and water available).

items.stem: With the help of a specific example, explain why some high-income countries have ecological footprints far above their biocapacity.
items.answer: High per-capita consumption of energy, meat and goods combined with limited domestic land means they rely on imports and the global atmosphere, e.g. Japan or the UK run large ecological deficits. (A specific, correct example that illustrates this is required for full marks.)

items.answer: It means demand exceeds annual regeneration; the rest of the year is met by depleting stocks and accumulating CO₂.

items.stem: Briefly explain why the Green Revolution is often used to challenge Malthusian views.
items.answer: High-yielding varieties, irrigation, fertilisers and pesticides from the 1960s more than doubled cereal yields in Asia and Latin America, so food supply grew faster than population, as Boserup predicted.

items.stem: Distinguish between water consumption and water withdrawal.
items.answer: Withdrawal is water removed from a source, some of which returns (e.g. cooling water); consumption is water used up and not returned, e.g. evaporated in irrigation or incorporated in products.

items.stem: Briefly explain why global energy consumption has continued to rise despite efficiency gains.
items.answer: Population growth and rising incomes in Asia and Africa increase demand for electricity, transport and industry; efficiency gains are offset by more use (the rebound effect).

items.answer: Irrigated farming feeds large rural populations in dry or monsoonal climates (India, Pakistan, Egypt), and industry and domestic supply networks are smaller; in high-income countries industry and power plants take a larger share.

items.stem: Explain how Boserup's theory differs from Malthus's theory.
items.answer: Malthus saw food supply as the limit to population; Boserup argued that population growth drives agricultural change (shorter fallow, irrigation, terracing), so food supply responds to population.

items.stem: Explain why rising consumption in emerging economies has global consequences.
items.answer: Increased demand raises world prices for food, energy and minerals, increases emissions and pressure on land and water, and changes trade flows (e.g. China's soy imports from Brazil).

items.stem: Give one strength and one weakness of the claim that the growth of the global middle class is a greater threat to resource security than population growth.
items.answer: Rising affluence is currently the stronger driver, but population growth multiplies its effect.
items.markingKey: For: per-capita consumption rises steeply with income (meat, cars, energy). Against: population growth in Africa will add over a billion people. [4]: 1 mark for a valid argument for, 1 for its development; 1 mark for a valid argument against, 1 for its development; generic points without geographical context are capped at 2.

items.stem:
Study the infographic / visual stimulus described below.

Pie chart description: global freshwater withdrawals by sector - agriculture 70%; industry 19%; domestic 11%. Total about 4,000 km³ per year.

(a) Calculate the volume used by agriculture. [4]
(b) Using the resource and your own knowledge, suggest how the pie chart for a high-income country such as Germany might differ. [6]
items.answer: (a) 0.70 × 4,000 = 2,800 km³ per year (b) A much smaller agricultural share and a much larger industrial share (power-station cooling), because farming is rain-fed and industry is large.
items.markingKey: (a) 0.70 × 4,000 = 2,800 km³ per year (b) A much smaller agricultural share and a much larger industrial share (power-station cooling), because farming is rain-fed and industry is large. Credit relevant own knowledge and named examples in (b). items.stem:
Study the infographic / visual stimulus described below.

Table: ecological footprint and biocapacity (global hectares per person, recent year) - USA 8.0, 3.4; China 3.7, 0.9; Brazil 2.6, 8.6; India 1.2, 0.4; world 2.6, 1.5.

(a) Calculate the ecological balance for each country and state whether it is a reserve or deficit. [4]
(b) Using the resource and your own knowledge, calculate how many Earths would be needed if everyone lived like the average US resident (world biocapacity 1.5 gha). [6]
items.answer: (a) USA −4.6 (deficit); China −2.8 (deficit); Brazil +6.0 (reserve); India −0.8 (deficit); world −1.1 (deficit). (b) 8.0 / 1.5 ≈ 5.3 Earths
items.markingKey: (a) USA −4.6 (deficit); China −2.8 (deficit); Brazil +6.0 (reserve); India −0.8 (deficit); world −1.1 (deficit). (b) 8.0 / 1.5 ≈ 5.3 Earths Credit relevant own knowledge and named examples in (b). items.stem: Evaluate the claim that the growth of the global middle class is a greater threat to resource security than population growth.
items.answer: Rising affluence is currently the stronger driver, but population growth multiplies its effect.
items.markingKey: Indicative content - for: per-capita consumption rises steeply with income (meat, cars, energy); middle-class growth is concentrated where populations are already large (China, India). Against / limitations: population growth in Africa will add over a billion people; technology and efficiency can reduce per-capita resource use. A supported conclusion might be: Rising affluence is currently the stronger driver, but population growth multiplies its effect. items.stem: Which term matches this description: "The capacity of ecosystems in an area to regenerate resources and absorb wastes, measured in global hectares"?
items.answer: biocapacity
items.markingKey: C. This is the definition of biocapacity.

items.stem: Outline the meaning of the term "purchasing power parity (PPP)".
items.answer: An exchange rate that adjusts for differences in the cost of living, allowing fair comparison of incomes between countries
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: an exchange rate that adjusts for differences in the cost of living, allowing fair comparison of incomes between countries. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Approximately what share of global freshwater withdrawals is used by agriculture?
items.answer: About 70%
items.markingKey: C. Industry uses about 19% and domestic uses about 11% (FAO AQUASTAT).

items.stem: Explain why the ecological footprint is a useful but limited measure of resource consumption.
items.answer: It converts diverse consumption into one comparable area (gha) and compares it with biocapacity, but it omits some impacts (toxic pollution, freshwater use), depends on assumptions and treats carbon only as forest land needed to absorb it.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: It converts diverse consumption into one comparable area (gha) and compares it with biocapacity, but it omits some impacts (toxic pollution, freshwater use), depends on assumptions and treats carbon only as forest land needed to absorb it. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: "Population growth is the only cause of rising global resource use." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Rising per-capita consumption from growing incomes has been as important as population growth, especially in Asia.
items.markingKey: Rising per-capita consumption from growing incomes has been as important as population growth, especially in Asia. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Tariq writes: "Energy use is similar in all high-income countries." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Per-capita use varies widely: Canada and the USA use about twice as much as Germany or Japan because of climate, distance, lifestyle and prices.
items.markingKey: Per-capita use varies widely: Canada and the USA use about twice as much as Germany or Japan because of climate, distance, lifestyle and prices. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: A student claims: "Earth Overshoot Day means the world runs out of resources on that date." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: It means demand exceeds annual regeneration; the rest of the year is met by depleting stocks and accumulating CO₂.
items.markingKey: It means demand exceeds annual regeneration; the rest of the year is met by depleting stocks and accumulating CO₂. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Distinguish between total consumption and consumption per capita.
items.answer: Per-capita consumption is the average used by each person; total consumption is per-capita use multiplied by population - China's total is large even though per-capita use is below the USA's.
items.markingKey: Per-capita consumption is the average used by each person; total consumption is per-capita use multiplied by population - China's total is large even though per-capita use is below the USA's. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Distinguish between non-renewable energy and renewable energy.
items.answer: Renewable energy (solar, wind, hydro) is naturally replenished; non-renewable energy (fossil fuels, uranium) comes from finite stocks that are depleted by use.
items.markingKey: Renewable energy (solar, wind, hydro) is naturally replenished; non-renewable energy (fossil fuels, uranium) comes from finite stocks that are depleted by use. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Bangladesh: ecological footprint ≈ 0.8 gha/person; biocapacity ≈ 0.4 gha/person. World biocapacity is about 1.6 gha per person. Calculate (a) the ecological balance per person and (b) how many Earths would be needed if everyone lived like the average resident.
items.answer: (a) -0.4 gha per person (ecological deficit) (b) 0.8 / 1.6 ≈ 0.5 Earths
items.markingKey: (a) M1 biocapacity − footprint, A1 -0.4 gha and correct label. (b) M1 A1 0.5 Earths.

items.stem:
The following information is provided.

Bar chart description: average meat consumption (kg per person per year) - USA 124; Brazil 100; China 63; Japan 50; India 4; Nigeria 9.

Suggest two reasons for the variation.
items.answer: Income levels (the USA, Brazil high); cultural and religious factors (vegetarianism and taboos on beef in India); availability and price of livestock products.
items.markingKey: Income levels (the USA, Brazil high); cultural and religious factors (vegetarianism and taboos on beef in India); availability and price of livestock products. Award 1 mark per valid point or correct step, up to [3]; data quoted must include units; points must be drawn from the resource.

items.stem: Water Footprint Network averages: rice 2,500 L per kg, beef 15,400 L per kg, cotton T-shirt (250 g) 2,700 L per shirt. Calculate the virtual water embedded in a weekly purchase by a student in Singapore of 3 kg of rice, 0.5 kg of beef, 1 cotton T-shirt (250 g). Explain why virtual water trade matters for water-scarce importing countries.
items.answer: 17,900 litres; importing water-intensive goods lets scarce countries (e.g. Jordan, Egypt) "save" domestic water, but creates dependence on exporters.
items.markingKey: M1 multiplying each quantity by its water content; A1 17,900 L. R1 virtual-water explanation.

items.stem:
Study the infographic / visual stimulus described below.

Table: share of world population in extreme poverty (World Bank, %) - 1990: 38.0; 2000: 29.3; 2010: 16.2; 2019: 8.9.

(a) Calculate the percentage fall in the extreme poverty rate between 1990 and 2019. [4]
(b) Using the resource and your own knowledge, describe the trend and suggest one reason why it has slowed since 2019. [6]
items.answer: (a) (8.9 − 38.0)/38.0 × 100 = -76.6% (b) A steady, rapid fall; since 2019 progress stalled because of COVID-19, conflict and food and energy price shocks, and because the remaining poor are concentrated in fragile states.

items.stem: To what extent do you agree that Malthus's ideas are still relevant to the 21st century?
items.answer: Malthus's simple model was wrong about food, but neo-Malthusian concerns about environmental limits remain relevant.
items.markingKey: Indicative content - for: climate change, soil degradation and water scarcity may limit food supply; the global footprint exceeds biocapacity (about 1.7 Earths). Against / limitations: food production has outpaced population since 1798; fertility is falling globally; technology and trade raise carrying capacity. A supported conclusion might be: Malthus's simple model was wrong about food, but neo-Malthusian concerns about environmental limits remain relevant.
